Sports.title: Manchester City's 115: What the charges mean and what happens now
Sports.text:
It has taken more than two years, but a judgement finally appears to have been reached on the 115 charges levelled against Manchester City over breaches of Premier League financial rules.

Following a four-year investigation, City were charged and the hearing finally got under way on 16 September 2024.

BBC Sport has now learned a decision has been made, after the Athletic reported City had been found guilty on all almost of the charges.

We are not at the end of this process, however. Far from it.

But what does this mean for City's titles? What about their Premier League status? Will there be an appeal? And how long will it be before this saga does come to an end?

German newspaper Der Spiegel published leaked documents, including emails purportedly sent between top City executives (some of whom remain at the City Football Group), across several seasons following the club's Abu Dhabi takeover in 2008.

It alleged these showed the club had inflated sponsorship revenue from state-owned airline Etihad and state-controlled telecoms firm Etisalat by disguising direct investment from their holding company (Sheik Mansour's Abu Dhabi United Group, or ADUG) as sponsorship income by channelling the funds through the companies' accounts.

This, it was alleged, was a means of meeting FFP rules introduced by Uefa in 2011 - and PSR brought in by the Premier League in 2012 - limiting clubs' permitted losses.

There then followed further allegations of misreporting financial information centred on documents that claimed to show secret 'off-the-books' payments to then manager Roberto Mancini via consultancy fees from a club in Abu Dhabi.

It is also alleged the club gave players more money than was officially going through the accounts so recorded spending was less than it actually was.

City, who have always maintained ADUG is a private fund rather than an arm of the state, refused to comment on any of Der Spiegel's revelations, saying the leaked emails were obtained illegally, and they were an "attempt to damage the club's reputation".

City - along with the companies involved - strongly denied breaking any financial rules. But that did not stop both Uefa and the Premier League launching investigations as a result.

November 2018: Football Leaks allegations emerge with Der Spiegel publishing claims Manchester City breached financial fair play rules.

March 2019: Uefa launches a formal investigation off the back of Der Spiegel's findings.

May 2019: City criticise the investigation and launch an appeal process.

November 2019: The Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) deems City's appeal inadmissible.

February 2020: Uefa announces a two-year ban for City from European competitions and a €30m fine.

July 2020: City's European ban is overturned after an appeal to Cas.

July 2021: City lose a jurisdiction ruling that allows the media to report the Premier League is continuing to investigate the champions for alleged financial breaches.

April 2022: Der Spiegel publishes a fresh report claiming the Premier League has been investigating the club for three years, providing detailed claims.

February 2023: The Premier League charges City with 115 financial breaches.

September 2024: The start of a 10-week hearing between the Premier League and City on the 115 charges.

February 2025: City manager Pep Guardiola says the club expect to learn the verdict "within one month". Guardiola left the Etihad at the end of last season.

September 2026: Reports emerge that a verdict has been reached, with sources telling the BBC that City have been found guilty of breaking the majority of the charges.

It was never expected the verdict would come complete with the sanctions.

We now face a waiting game for even that verdict to officially be made public by the independent panel.

We don't know who was on the panel that heard and ruled on the case, and that will only come once a written judgment is released.

All options are open to the disciplinary commission:

Points deduction (immediate or suspended).

Financial penalties (immediate or suspended).

Removal from the Premier League.

Being removed from the Premier League would mean City lose their membership and are demoted to a lower division from the end of the season.

That could also happen through a points penalty so severe they would effectively be relegated.

The Premier League declined to comment on the case when approached on Friday.

City issued a statement that showed frustration news of the verdict had leaked.

It read: "The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality.

"As such Manchester City FC's position remains consistent with the club's statement of February 2023.

"The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence."

An appeal from City is expected to be a formality.

City's legal team is being led by Lord Pannick KC, who is reported to charge £5,000 an hour for his services. He helped City overturn their two-year European ban in 2020.

However, considering we are already eight years into this process - and two years beyond the start of the hearing itself - it is impossible to speculate when this could come to an end.

Until now, the case has been watertight, with no media leaks from any of the parties involved.

This is just the latest chapter.

However, while the commission's judgement can be directly appealed against, it is not possible for City to take it to Cas.

This specific case was six years in the making, so legal fees on both sides were estimated at tens of millions of pounds before the hearing even started.

Whichever side 'wins' can be expected to make a claim for costs.

For context, the Premier League wanted Everton to pay the full £4.9m legal costs of their first PSR six-point deduction case.

However, an appeal board ruled Everton should pay £1.7m and the Premier League cover the remaining £3.2m legal fees.

Any costs being paid by the Premier League at the end of the City case would have to be spread across the 20 clubs which make up the league.

Comparisons have been drawn to the cases brought by the Premier League against Nottingham Forest and Everton respectively over breaches of PSR.

During the 2023-24 season, both clubs were docked points for making more losses than they were permitted to for the three-year period from the 2020-21 to 2022-23 seasons.

Those cases were of a single charge, were easier to decipher and involved significantly less evidence.

Everton were twice deducted points. For the first charge, they were docked six points - reduced from 10 points on appeal. The second offence led to them being handed a two-point penalty.

Forest, meanwhile, lost four points.

However, these relate purely to PSR.

Chelsea faced 74 charges of rule breaches, but these were quite different and primarily focused on transfers that happened between the 2010-11 and 2015-16 seasons, including deals for Eden Hazard, Samuel Eto'o and Willian.

The Premier League fined Chelsea £10m and handed out a suspended transfer ban after they admitted making £47m in secret payments.

Importantly, Chelsea reached a settlement with the Premier League in relation to historical regulatory matters that were self-reported.

This has not been the case with City, who have always denied wrongdoing.

The Blues were also fined by Uefa and the Football Association.

Sports.title: Sir David Beckham nets £38.5m after World Cup ad deals
Sports.text:
Sir David Beckham has netted a £38.5m payout from his sports, fashion, and media business after the 2026 Men's Football World Cup helped it bring in record profits.

The former England star's DRJB Holdings, which includes the Beckham brand, reported an almost £50m profit in 2025, a 46% jump compared to a year earlier. Sales rose from £72.2m to £84m.

The rise was driven by a slew of advertising partnerships struck in the runup to the tournament, including with Bank of America, McDonald's, Verizon, and PepsiCo Lay's.

Sir David, Britain's first billionaire sportsman, was commonly seen in adverts during the summer's World Cup.

In the US, it was difficult for fans to watch a game without coming across Beckham in adverts for Stella Artois, Home Depot and Lay's crisps - known as Walkers in the UK.

Sir David also launched menswear collections for Hugo Boss last year, as well as a pair of Adidas Predator football boots and an eyewear range with Italian glasses maker Safilo.

Revenues at DRJB, of which Beckham owns almost half, were boosted by growth in Beckham's health supplements business too.

DRJB paid its shareholders £38.9m, followed by a special £46.6m payment after the end of the financial year.

Sir David's share of those dividends would have been around £38.5m due to how much of the company he owns.

The remainder of DRJB is owned by New York-based Authentic Brands Group, which also owns Reebok, as well as the rights to other celebrity brands such as comedian and actor Kevin Hart.

Authentic's entertainment chief executive Corey Salter said the performance showed Sir David's name is "one of the most powerful global brands in sport, lifestyle, entertainment and much more".

"It's been an outstanding year, from new partnerships to important philanthropic campaigns and overall brand growth," he said.

Sir David previously drew criticism for associating himself with a country where same-sex relationships are illegal by acting as an ambassador for the 2022 Men's Football World Cup in Qatar.

"It was an important competition and one I was proud to be part of," he said at the time, adding that he had engaged with the LGBTQ community during the tournament.

Sports.title: Cole Palmer misses too many opportunities to play for England - Thomas Tuchel
Sports.text:
Cole Palmer "misses too many opportunities" to play for England after the Chelsea forward pulled out of the latest squad, says manager Thomas Tuchel.

The withdrawal of Palmer came as a surprise as he has started all five of Chelsea's matches in the Premier League so far this season, though Tuchel says he had been playing with "discomfort and pain".

The 24-year-old was left out of the World Cup squad by Tuchel and has featured just three times since the German took charge of the Three Lions in January 2025.

"My understanding is that he is playing with discomfort and pain, and he cannot compete at the highest level with discomfort and pain. So he withdrew and informed us, and Chelsea informed us." Tuchel said.

"For sure. It is a missed opportunity. He misses too many opportunities. I don't blame him for it. It is just a fact.

"He misses way too many camps with injuries, and I only want to rely on what I witness and see within in my team, and for that you have to be in camp.

"And if you're not in camp, there is a next level to impress that you cannot achieve because you can only do it when you are actually on the pitch with me. So yes, it is a missed opportunity."

It is understood Palmer is currently abroad completing an injury-specific training plan.

Chelsea's non international players have been given days off and have been permitted to travel if they so wish.

Palmer has been accompanied by a Chelsea rehabilitation coach on his overseas trip.

Declan Rice, Tino Livramento, Marcus Rashford and Kobbie Mainoo are the other players who pulled out with injury.

Tuchel said he was not worried that players may put their clubs above playing for their country.

"We are not managing load. When I was in club football, I used the term 'international break' and, when you hear it from the other side, it is a totally different picture," he said.

"It is a competitive environment, but it is also an environment that the players love to be a part of.

"That is what togetherness and brotherhood look like, and that is what we have created since last September in qualifying. We will never compromise on that.

"We will never let it creep in that we have a feeling players do not want to come. We focus on the guys who absolutely want to play for England."

Sports.title: Azerbaijan Grand Prix: Russell takes pole as Antonelli out after hitting wall
Sports.text:
George Russell took an imperious pole position for Mercedes at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix as his team-mate and championship leader Kimi Antonelli crashed out.

Russell beat Ferrari's Charles Leclerc by a massive 0.837 seconds while Antonelli, who leads the Britain by 81 points in the championship, will start in 16th.

The Italian hit the inside wall at Turn One in the first session and was knocked out.

McLaren's Oscar Piastri was third ahead of Red Bull's Isack Hadjar and McLaren's Lando Norris.

Lewis Hamilton, compromised by running without a tow from another car, was sixth, ahead of the Alpine of Pierre Gasly and Red Bull's Max Verstappen.

With a tow or slipstream worth as much as 0.5 seconds, Verstappen was following Norris on their final laps when the Briton made a mistake and went off track.

That scuppered Verstappen's chances of competing closer to the front.

But although the four-time champion said he believed he could have been on the front row, he acknolweged that he could not have beaten Russell.

On a weekend in which Antonelli's running has been compromised by reliability problems that meant he missed out on half the possible running on Thursday, Russell absolutely delivered on Mercedes' dominant position on this unique track.

Russell has looked comfortable all weekend and never looked in danger of being beaten for pole, his first since the Austrian Grand Prix at the end of June.

"That's probably the biggest margin I've had in my whole career," Russell said. "The lap felt really sweet and the car has been feeling great all weekend."

Leclerc was somewhat taken aback by Mercedes' superiority, saying that the position was what he expected but the gap most definitely was not.

At the bottom of the top 10, there was finally some good news for Williams, for whom Carlos Sainz achieved the team's first top 10 qualifying performance of the year with ninth on the grid.

However, the Spaniard was later penalised for failing to slow for yellow caution flags and was given a five-place penalty.

Williams have introduced a new chassis this weekend which has brought them down to the weight limit for the first time this season, after being as much as 25kg over at the start of the year.

Along with some additional developments, it appears to have produced a significant step forwards, although the caveat is that Baku is a track that suits the characteristics of the Williams car and does not expose its weaknesses.

Team-mate Alex Albon did not manage to secure a tow in the second part of qualifying, and was "anyway struggling with straight-line speed all session", and was 13th, just under 0.4secs behind the Spaniard. Sainz's penalty will promote him a place on the grid.

Antonelli's error came on his second lap of the first session.

He turned into the first corner too early, and the left front wheel clouted the inside wall, breaking the suspension.

He initially tried to get the car back to the pits but was told by engineer Peter Bonnington to park up.

"Let me try," Antonelli pleaded, before Bonnington told him that either the track rod or upright was broken and there was no way Mercedes could fix that in the time they had to turn the car around before the next session.

Antonelli had been on the back foot all Friday trying to catch up time lost to a hydraulic problem that had stopped his car on track halfway through first practice, and was not repaired until halfway into the second.

It was Antonelli's first major mistake of the season since he crashed heavily in final practice at the first race of the season in Australia.

Sports.title: Israel v Republic of Ireland: Jack Knight says Nations League game should not go ahead
Sports.text:
Jason Knight has become the first Republic of Ireland player to publicly voice his opposition to playing Israel on Sunday.

The sides are due to meet in Debrecen, Hungary at 19:45 BST, with the return fixture in Backa Topola, Serbia on 4 October.

Since the sides were drawn together in Group B3, there has been increasing calls in Ireland to withdraw from the games due to the ongoing war in Gaza with a 'Stop The Game' campaign gathering pace.

Speaking before Thursday's 1-0 defeat by Kosovo in Pristina, Republic stand-in skipper Dara O'Shea confirmed the players would meet on Friday to discuss their approach to Sunday's 'home' game against Israel, which will have no Irish fans in attendance, before their behind-closed-doors match the following week.

"Look, it's difficult, the manager, and Dara, and Nathan [Collins] spoke well about it, I don't think the game should be going ahead but it is going ahead," Knight said following the Kosovo game.

"We'll have a deeper talk about it and what that means, we'll get our thoughts as a group and go from there.

"I think it was a difficult one. It's obviously big talk in Ireland. I have been focusing on my football in England in the Championship. But I knew this was coming so I had a think about it."

Sports.title: Kevin Pietersen: Former England batter on Harry Brook and working with Test side before Ashes
Sports.text:
Kevin Pietersen is asked, after everything that came before, what he would have said if told he would work for the England and Wales Cricket board again one day.

In 2014, he was sacked by the ECB in one of most ugly and acrimonious periods in English cricketing history – a period that brought one of the most exciting but divisive international careers to an end.

"What do you think I'd have said," Pietersen says with a smile.

Bigger stars in English cricket are harder to find.

This is the man who had a brief but high-profile relationship with American celebrity Caprice, married a pop star, Jessica from Liberty X, and once tried to explain cricket to Taylor Swift on The Graham Norton Show.

Back in the dressing room as a mentor, he is speaking to the media at Headingley - the location of his famous "it's tough being me" press conference.

The hair is greyer, but he still carries all of that aura.

"I'm 46, man," he says, asked whether animosity remains.

"That stuff is so long gone. I am a completely different person.

"I live in South Africa. I love doing what I do. I am just here to help Brendon first and foremost, help the players try and become the best versions of themselves."

Pietersen was the most intriguing of appointments to England's dressing room staff because of his own history, but also what he has said before.

While commentating on England's white-ball tour of India last year, he suggested the Brendon McCullum outfit were not training enough.

"Clearly the perceptions I had before being asked to do the job were completely different to what I feel now," he says.

"It is nice to being part of an England team and set-up that is actually really, really driven."

Pietersen answers every question with poise. Almost all are given and lengthy, considered responses.

His only terse response comes when pushed on what exactly those preconceptions were - and how quickly they took to disappear.

"You know what the preconceptions were," he says. "I am not going near it."

Despite that, he appears to be loving his return.

Pietersen is "not sitting here wanting to be the coach of England" but wants to help McCullum and the players, many of whom grew up idolising him.

One of those, Tom Banton, said last week he is still in awe of the four-time Ashes-winner, so much so he was struggling to build up the courage to speak to him.

"He wants a YouTube channel," Pietersen laughs. Pietersen, a 50-over great who played in a way ahead of his time, can also help him there.

His official title is "specialist mentor" and he will dip in and out to work with the white-ball teams through to the 50-over World Cup next autumn.

Before the first ODI in Durham, England posted a clip on social media of Pietersen leading a batting session.

Holding court, he had Joe Root and Rehan Ahmed alike involved in a batting drill on how to rotate the strike against spin.

"All I want to be is a great person to these guys," Pietersen says.

"I want to be the best guy in the room, so that they come to me, and they ask me for information, and if I've got stuff for them, I'll give it to them.

"I am lucky to have worn every T-shirt an England cricketer can wear – the good, the bad the ugly.

"I can potentially help them to stay away from the ugly."

Pietersen's eyes roll slightly when he is asked about Ben Stokes' recent comments comparing Harry Brook's talents to his.

Pietersen, like Brook, was a maverick – a batter capable of incredible highs. Those highs mean the lows come with a disproportionate level of criticism.

"Where I can help him is playing situations, because there was a lot of method in my madness," Pietersen says.

"Yes, occasionally, I got out to reckless shots and crazy shots in the '80s and '90s but there was a lot of structure to the way that I batted.

"I've still got notes on my phone on how I played in T20 cricket, one-day cricket, Test match cricket, and about hitting straight back at the stumps, and the techniques, and how I did it, and don't play certain shots.

"That all-round structure is something I could potentially help him with because he's so flipping good.

"It's actually frightening how good he is and how good he can be."

And Pietersen says he will not limit himself to working purely on white-ball cricket.

He has already spoken to new Test coach Stephen Fleming about how he can help the Test batters during his time with the white-ball squads.

Though he said he would not have time for a full-time role, he suggested he is open to working with the Test side before next summer's home Ashes series.

"I have got a pretty mad schedule," he says. "I wouldn't say no.

"I don't think that necessarily means I need to be in a dressing room.

"There is a lot of time in the lead up to an Ashes series and a tour of South Africa, when I will be with the Test batters.

"There are conversations I can have there."

Who knows how long this will last. England may as well make the most of this second chance.

Sports.title: FA Cup: Mulbarton Wanderers and Woodford Town must replay qualifying tie after referee's error
Sports.text:
An FA Cup tie between Mulbarton Wanderers and Woodford Town is making the headlines because of a refereeing error which has caused a replay.

So what sets this apart from other matches impacted by an error from officials? And could we see it happen in leagues which have the video assistant referee (VAR)?

For example, there were 25 VAR errors last season. This season an error has already been publicly acknowledged after Manchester United lost 1-0 at home to Manchester City.

Mulbarton, who won the tie 2-1 on the day, say they are "deeply upset" after their opponents lodged a protest because a goal scored from a penalty was ruled out.

The referee disallowed Woodford's goal for encroachment by a number of attacking players and awarded Mulbarton an indirect free-kick.

Law 14 states, external that the referee should have ordered the penalty to be retaken.

A Football Association sub-committee found there had been a technical error by the referee and ordered the match to be replayed on Tuesday.

So deciding if a game should be replayed comes down to whether a referee has made a simple subjective judgement call, or whether the decision should not have been given because it is not part of the laws of the game.

Mulbarton, who play in the Isthmian League North, claim the decision to replay the game could lead to "wider implications regarding the finality of results" and the "integrity of the game as a whole".

Yet matches being replayed because of a misapplication of the laws is more common than you might think, and it can happen for a variety of reasons.

A Spartan South Midlands League fixture between Edgware Town and Harefield United in 2006 is thought to be the first in English football to be ordered to be replayed, external because of a referee's error.

It was a carbon copy of the Mulbarton-Woodford situation. Edgware scored a penalty, the referee spotted encroachment by the attacking team and gave an indirect free-kick to Harefield. It should have been a retake.

Ordering a replay is far more likely to happen in a cup game, as the incorrect decision is considered to have had a direct impact on the outcome of a competition tie. In the league, it is just one match of a season-long tournament.

Uefa made such a judgment for the first time in 2015 following a European Championship qualifier between England Under-19 women's team and Norway.

Trailing 2-1, Leah Williamson scored England's stoppage time spot-kick, but the goal was disallowed because of attacking encroachment. Again, it should have been a retake.

Uefa ordered the match to be restarted from the moment of the penalty, and the players reconvened five days later. Williamson scored from the spot, the game finished 2-2 and it took England to the Euros.

There are other recent examples in England, too. An FA Vase tie was replayed last season after a referee's error over a penalty shootout.

Last year, Bridlington Town were forced to replay their 2-1 FA Cup win against Knaresborough through no fault of their own. The refereeing team was wrong in law to refuse Knaresborough a fifth substitute during extra time.

Crucially, it cannot just be a matter of subjective opinion or judgement - like getting a corner wrong, or awarding a disputed penalty.

With the laws on encroachment relaxed in recent years, now requiring it to cause clear impact on an opponent, there was little case for an offence by Woodford.

With the goal being scored, the only offence possible would be the encroaching attackers having put off the goalkeeper. It would be a stretch but still subjective.

But even if you could justify the decision to disallow the goal, the restart should have been a retake. Other than the kicker committing illegal feinting, there was nothing in the laws about giving an indirect free-kick.

Redbridge-based Woodford said the decision "ensures the tie can be concluded in accordance with FA Cup rules".

The winners will host Gloucester City of the Southern League Premier Division South in the third qualifying round on Saturday, 3 October.

The International Football Association Board is clear when it comes to mistakes by the video official.

It states a match is not invalidated because of "wrong decision(s) involving the VAR".

Let's take the goal in the Manchester derby.

The VAR, Matt Donohue, did not make a judgement on the potential offside offence by Fernandez.

Even then, this would still be a subjective assessment of Fernandez's impact on United's Lisandro Martinez and goalkeeper Senne Lammens.

Even if Donohue had properly looked at it, this would not be considered a misapplication of the law, but just a mistake.

The same would apply to Luis Diaz's disallowed 'offside goal' for Liverpool at Tottenham three years ago.

The VAR, Darren England, came to the correct decision in law, but communicated this to the referee incorrectly. This is not considered an error of the laws of the game.

In July 2020, the operator of the Premier League's goalline technology system had to apologise after an error denied Sheffield United a goal in their 0-0 draw at Aston Villa.

Villa goalkeeper Orjan Nyland carried Oliver Norwood's 42nd-minute free-kick over the line but referee Michael Oliver did not receive a signal to indicate a goal.

Also buried within VAR protocol is a clause which states "malfunction(s) of the VAR technology" cannot invalidate a result.

There was a fascinating case in the Eredivisie in December 2024.

PEC Zwolle's late winner against RKC Waalwijk was ruled out for offside. The problem? The offside was given from a corner, which was not possible under the laws.

A number of appeals failed, with the Dutch FA saying that the referee applied the rules correctly and only an incorrect judgment was made.

Perhaps the best case study comes from the Belgian Pro League in December 2023.

The incident occurred in Genk's 2-1 defeat by Anderlecht when Yira Sor scored a rebound from a missed penalty.

The VAR disallowed the goal because Sor encroached in the area but the video official did not identify encroachment by two Anderlecht players. It should have been a retake rather than a free-kick.

Genk successfully protested for a replay based on the laws being "misapplied".

Belgium's Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned that decision and the result stood. Its reasoning gives good insight.

It said that the decision was not "a violation of the laws" and just "carelessness in the assessment of the game situation".

You could apply both to Fernandez and Diaz.

"Football clubs must realise that referees are not robots and, just like footballers themselves, make mistakes," the court added.

A decision in Belgium does not, of course, have any bearing in the Premier League, or any other competition with VAR.

But we are not about to see a raft of appeals against results just because of the misapplication of the law in some cup games.

Sports.title: How will Sebastien Pocognoli's new-look Scotland squad line-up?
Sports.text:
Showtime is fast approaching for Sebastien Pocognoli's Scotland.

The Tartan Army are taking over the Slovenian capital of Ljubljana and their heroes will join them later on Friday when they fly in from La Manga for Saturday's opening Nations League game.

Scotland's new head coach took a fair few fresh faces out to Spain, something that earned him early kudos from supporters who were calling for a bit of shake-up in the squad - but how does that translate to his team?

Adding eight uncapped players to a 27-man squad - before releasing Findlay Curtis and James Wilson to the under-21s - is one thing, but will the line-up reflect such a shift when it drops on the national team's social media channels on Saturday afternoon?

Former Scotland winger Pat Nevin thinks it would be "slightly bizarre" to see any more than two uncapped starters, while his fellow ex-international, James McFadden, insists the team will look "pretty similar" without any "big surprises".

So is it a case of the more things change, the more they stay the same for Scotland?

Going by what we know of Pocognoli's past, many are leading with the assumption he will play a back-three in defence.

The addition of Stephen Welsh, Luke Graham and Luis Binks - all new to the Scotland set-up - perhaps offers a sneak-peak as to what could come further down the line, but for now, will it be a more tried and trusted trio?

Jack Hendry and Scott McKenna - although the latter now does have left-footed competition in Graham and Binks - appear to be favoured by most, but what of the the right centre-back?

McFadden thinks pushing Brentford right-back Aaron Hickey there will help "drive" the team forward.

"I hope the centre-backs aren't the players on the team who have the ball the most," the former Scotland forward said on the BBC's Scottish Football Podcast.

"I don't want to see this centre-back to centre-back play. If they're getting it, I want them to drive and I think, if you had Hickey as a right-centre-back, he'd be driving into the play and trying to commit to going forward.

"I don't want them just sitting in a safe position, playing around the back. I don't want to see that, it's boring."

One player who is seldom boring for Scotland is Billy Gilmour.

The midfielder's presence was missed at the World Cup, but after signing off from Serie A at the weekend with a goal for Napoli, he is returning ready to go.

Nevin will be making a swift exit from the Stozice Stadium if Gilmour is not starting - where he will surely be beside Lewis Ferguson.

"One of, if not the best player for us at the World Cup," McFadden said of the Bologna captain, who will surely look to his left and find captain Andy Robertson at wing-back.

"You're not going to go and change the midfield up. I don't think there's a need for a change for change's sake.

"I think that the freshness was needed, but I'm just looking forward to seeing them actually play and see if there's any difference in how they approach it - if they are more aggressive in a press and more dominant with possession."

Central to that will be John McGinn.

At times, Scotland have struggled to get the Aston Villa captain in his best position in midfield - and yet he still never fails to perform.

With Scott McTominay missing from the squad as he recovers from successful minor heart surgery, Nevin suggested: "We need his explosiveness in the final third, so I would like to see him a little bit further forward."

It is the same old names so far - with Bournemouth winger Ben Gannon-Doak operating somewhere down the right, dependent on Hickey's position - but we do know there will need to be a new-ish name up top of sorts.

Even still, the favourite to lead the line is 16-time capped, Oli McBurnie.

His exile from international football does mean he feels like a new addition - as does his words about his desire to perform on his long-awaited return.

"He's coming back with a point to prove, which I like," McFadden said.

"You've got someone who will give their all, which is how Oli plays anyway, and he'll feel privileged that he's got the opportunity to play again.

"It's a big opportunity, because over the last couple of years we've been so used to seeing Che Adams, Lyndon Dykes and Lawrence Shankland, so it'll be nice to see a bit of freshness up there."

That all leaves one spot up for grabs and, in this case, it's on the left of the front three. And Bournemouth's Ryan Christie is familiar with that responsibility.

Sports.title: Rangers: 100 days of Derek McInnes at Ibrox
Sports.text:
Derek McInnes has been in charge for 100 days at Rangers - the club he grew up supporting, played for and previously turned down the opportunity to manage.

In his brief but busy tenure, there has been a huge squad overhaul, while a sluggish start led to Ibrox jeers and the failure to qualify for European football for the first time in a decade.

Then came September. A golden start to autumn quietened talk of crisis as a winning streak extended to six games, including two Old Firm derby victories.

BBC Sport Scotland charts the key moments of McInnes' reign.

One month and one day after his Heart of Midlothian side were pipped to the title by Celtic on the final day of last season, McInnes is announced as Rangers manager, replacing the departed Danny Rohl.

It is 26 years since his days as a Rangers player ended with a move to West Bromwich Albion and eight-and-a-half years since he turned down the chance to become boss under the chairmanship of Dave King.

"It is no secret that I grew up a Rangers supporter and I am convinced this is the right time to take on this prestigious role," McInnes says. "There is a lot of hard work ahead."

The new era begins at Tannadice with a whimper rather than a bang as Thelo Aasgaard scores a second-half equaliser in a 1-1 draw with Dundee United.

"We worked hard to get back into it, but I don't think we were good enough to win the game," McInnes says. "I thought the point was the right scoreline and we're disappointed with that first half.

"We wasted a lot, we didn't create too much and it was a bit too frantic."

Curtain up on Rangers European campaign - and it does not start well.

A trip to eastern Poland in the first leg of their Europa League third qualifying round tie ends in a 2-1 defeat by Jagellonia Bialystok.

McInnes notes: "I just felt we beat ourselves, to be honest. We got off to a good start, being patient with what we were trying to do. We made two mistakes for the two goals."

Rangers' first home match of the season ends also ends in a 2-1 defeat, this time by Hibernian.

A late Callum Wright goal seals victory for the Edinburgh side and, to make matters worse, striker Youseff Chermitti suffers an ACL injury that scuppers any potential big-money sale amid reports of interest from Galatasaray.

"There are little things going against us at the minute, but we have to stay strong - we're not as bad as people think," McInnes insists. "At the minute, we are trying to work boys back to the same level of fitness and trying to manage that situation.

"I understand the fan frustration. They want and expect to see their team win. I share the frustration."

Another below-par performance has supporters up in arms.

Shankland scores from the penalty spot, but a second-half goal from Nik Prelec earns Jagellonia a draw on the night and progress on aggregate.

McInnes confesses: "It is not great to watch. My team go from some good highs in the first half to being as poor as we were in the second half and you have to say we didn't do enough. We should be winning this game."

Five games into the new season and Rangers record their first win under McInnes - an emphatic 5-1 thumping of holders St Mirren in the Premier Sports Cup.

"We gave up a couple of chances, which we weren't too pleased about, but there was a good attacking threat from the team," McInnes concludes.

"The players deserved that moment today against a St Mirren team who have been doing well."

A penalty shoot-out defeat by the unfancied Czechs eliminates Rangers from Europe altogether.

Missed spot kicks by Findlay Curtis and James Penrice hand victory to Jablonec after a 1-0 defeat. A bitter blow for the balance sheet too as the Ibrox club face up to life without European football proper for the first time in 10 years.

"I'm embarrassed with the performance," McInnes says. "I think the only people who represented the club well tonight were my support staff and the supporters who, to a man, were outstanding, getting behind the team despite watching what we all watched."

McInnes registers his first Scottish Premiership win as Rangers manager at his old stamping ground of Pittodrie.

A Shankland penalty gets the job done, much to McInnes' relief as he praises Kim Min-Su as evidence that the summer recruitment is beginning to bear fruit.

"It was a tough few days for us all," he says. "I thought we were far more like the Rangers team I want us to be."

After a 2-1 success at Falkirk, a third successive Premiership win, but it comes at a cost as Shankland tears a hamstring against Motherwell at Ibrox and will be sidelined for months. Ryan Nederi replaces the captain and scores the only goal.

"We'd have taken any sort of win because we're up against a good team, but I really enjoyed how many chances we created," McInnes says.

Glasgow's big two meet again, this time at Celtic Park in the Premiership.

A Naderi goal stuns the 60,000 home supporters and moves Rangers two points behind their Glasgow rivals.

Afterwards, McInnes reflects: "It's just three points and it gets us three points closer to Celtic. We understood if we lost the game, that distance just starts to feel uncomfortable for us.

"I like putting my name to this team at the minute and I think we've got a good thing going."

Former Rangers interim boss and Captain Barry Ferguson

"I've been really impressed since exiting in Europe.

"I think the reaction, not just the manager and the coaching staff, the players, I've been very impressed. Even before the two Celtic games, they played well in parts of it, other parts they didn't, but they found a way to win, and that's so important.

"It's always going to take a bit of time because there was a big turnaround of players and some players hit the ground running.

"It takes some players a wee bit of time to get going. But now I think you're starting to see a team that's got a real togetherness. That's the biggest thing for me."

Sports.title: Billy Vigar: Parents say son's death could have been prevented
Sports.text:
"You swing from sadness to anger because you just feel it could have been prevented."

That is the view of Camilla Vigar, whose son Billy, a former Arsenal academy player, died a year ago today from a "significant brain injury", five days after colliding with a concrete wall surrounding a pitch.

The 21-year-old striker was playing for Chichester City at Wingate and Finchley FC in north London.

In their first broadcast interview since their son's passing, the Vigar family accuse the Football Association of doing "nothing" after previous similar incidents.

"[Billy] had his whole life ahead of him. He was 21 years old and he lost it playing football when he didn't need to," she told BBC Sport.

"I personally feel that the FA could have stopped Billy losing his life because they had so many warnings."

They give the example of amateur footballer Ben Hiscox, who died in 2015 after colliding with a clubhouse near Bristol.

After the coroner warned the FA about the risk of future deaths, padding was added to Stoke Gifford United's clubhouse and the run-off between it and the pitch was increased.

The Vigars also point to the life-changing injuries sustained by Alex Fletcher in 2022.

Fletcher fractured his skull when colliding with concrete barriers next to the pitch at Bath City's ground, and was forced to retire in 2024.

The FA conducted a review of clubs after that incident.

"As far as I'm aware, nothing was done with that information and it just sat there. One of the clubs as far as I'm aware that was highlighted as being one of the high-risk clubs was Wingate [and Finchley], where Billy then lost his life," said Camilla Vigar.

When asked by the BBC what was done with the information it had gathered, the FA provided no comment.

At the time of Vigar's accident, the FA's stadium accreditation criteria, which applies to the National League System in men's football and the Women's National League, said clubs needed to have a "permanent" barrier around the pitch "of sound construction (eg concrete and steel)".

In light of what happened to Vigar, the FA launched a safety review of more than 900 clubs, which was conducted by independent experts.

As a result, the stadium criteria was updated last month and "no longer permits solid brick, breeze block or concrete barriers around pitches".

The BBC has been told 169 clubs in the men's National League System and women's National League were notified they would need to make changes "as soon as is reasonably practicable".

Where walls are structural, they must be "covered with suitable protection", such as padding.

The FA said: "This important work is under way, and we will continue to fully support the clubs involved."

Funding is being provided by the FA and the Premier League.

BBC Sport approached hundreds of affected clubs in an effort to gauge their views on the changes and understand the status of their remedial work.

Bromsgrove Sporting near Birmingham, which has a concrete wall surrounding its pitch, told BBC Sport the changes were "completely understandable and long overdue". It added: "We are fully supportive of this and are grateful for the 100% funding from the FA."

The club said it had been given a deadline of the end of this season but "being high risk it would be good to complete this side of Christmas".

Meanwhile, Sheppey United, in Kent, has a concrete supporting wall around two sides of its 3G pitch, which will be covered in padding.

Asked for their thoughts on the changes, the club said: "There is always an element of risk in all sports and they can't all be mitigated, unfortunately in this instance the remedial works are more a reactive response rather than a proactive one. If the funding wasn't in place I think it would make it difficult for some clubs to fund this."

Bath City, where Fletcher's incident happened, has solid perimeter walls on all sides of its pitch.

The club told BBC Sport: "We welcome the ruling as it seeks to improve player safety and recognises that funding needs to be available to support clubs to implement this fundamental change to the ground grading regulations."

Keith Vigar, Billy's father, said: "I work in the health and safety industry, and the main thing is you don't go to work and expect to get injured, let alone even die at work in the workplace."

The Vigars want the regulations extended above and below the National League.

"It needs to change basically at all levels, not just at the levels that have changed," said Keith Vigar.

That is a view shared by Fletcher, who said the FA had "ignored" his years of campaigning on the issue of pitch perimeter safety.

"It wasn't until Billy's passing that [the FA] came to the table on this issue," he said.

"So for me, that is a complete dereliction of duty on their part, and there should be accountability for that failing."

Fletcher also said he is worried the ban on concrete, breeze block and brick walls does not cover all levels of the game and wants that explored urgently by the authorities.

"There could be still situations where football is being played at some level, to some degree, organised football in this country, with these unsafe pitch perimeters. I would like to see that guidance, or the regulation, extended to consider all of football."

Compared to many youngsters, Billy Vigar joined the football system late - and yet his talent was still recognised.

He was scouted by Arsenal while playing for local club Hove Rivervale in Sussex, and joined the Premier League side's academy.

"It was just an amazing feeling," said his father.

"Sort of like your son's been chosen. And I'd always promised him a decent pair of football boots if he joined an academy. So yeah, since then it's cost me a fortune.

"He was something different, Billy. I think most, even at Arsenal, they saw something different in him. He was a great athlete, basically. And that started from an early age with his brother, who quickly learned there's not much point trying to challenge him because he wanted to win."

Injuries followed, and Vigar was recuperating from one such setback while playing for Chichester City FC, where he had made an instant impression.

Darin Kilpatrick, the club's first-team manager, said: "He was so coachable, he would run in behind, he would drop in short. His hold-up play was excellent and obviously he had an eye for a goal which all strikers have to have.

"To be fair, the way Bills was playing in his last couple of games that we had him, we would probably have only been able to keep him another six months before we moved him on into the higher levels where he belonged."

Asked what level he was aiming for with Billy, Kilpatrick said: "He would have gone into the National League or [English] Football League, without a doubt."

Watching football again has been difficult for Keith Vigar.

"It did become less important, far less important to start with, the struggle to get back into it," he said. "When we went to see Chichester in that sense, first off, it's hard because you're just thinking, 'Billy should be out there, Billy should be playing' and that sort of thing. That's been hard."

The Vigars said Chichester FC have been "amazing" during the past year, including designing a kit that makes moving but subtle references to their son.

They want accountability and answers. They are awaiting the inquest, which is likely to take place next year.

But today, as they mark the one-year anniversary of their son's tragic accident, they will pour all their focus into climbing Snowdon with their children Phoebe and Ollie, and the family of Billy's girlfriend Lois.

"I think it just gives us something to focus on and gives us a challenge to do," Keith Vigar said. "And I know he'd have liked to do that. I'm sure he will be with us somewhere, looking over us in some way or form, having a laugh at us, no doubt, in the rain."

Sports.title: David Beckham takes £39m dividend as World Cup deals drive record profits
Sports.text:
David Beckham has taken a $51m (£39m) dividend from his business empire after a series of deals with brands for the Fifa World Cup.

Beckham appeared in about a dozen ad campaigns across this summer’s tournament in the US, working with brands including Lenovo, McDonald’s, Bank of America, Verizon and the PepsiCo crisps brand Lay’s.

The World Cup work helped to fuel a record year for DRJB Holdings, the commercial company for Beckham’s brands business, where revenues surged by a fifth to $110.5m last year, up from $92.3m in 2024.

Pre-tax profits also climbed to a record $65.7m, a 46% increase on 2024.

DRJB Holdings – which is made up of three divisions, the largest of which is DB Ventures, which covers most of his partnerships with brands such as Hugo Boss – paid out $51.1m to shareholders last year, compared with $53m the previous year.

The former England captain, who retired from professional football in 2013, sold a 55% stake in his businesses in 2022 to the US group Authentic Brands for £200m, meaning he took home 45% of last year’s total dividend.

However, the Companies House filing, which will be published next week, showed a further $61.6m was paid in special dividends this year. This meant Beckham was paid out about $51m.

Before this year’s World Cup the company secured partnerships including a multiyear deal with Bank of America: he became an ambassador for its global sports programme.

The 51-year-old also launched menswear collections for Hugo Boss, an eponymous range of spectacles for Safilo and a limited-edition Predator football boot with Adidas.

He also struck a new deal for Beckham & Friends Live, a show on Paramount+ that was broadcast around the Uefa Champions League.

Beckham featured in a Stella Artois campaign alongside the actor and producer Theo James to mark the beer’s partnership for the second season of Netflix series The Gentlemen.

DRJB Holdings is jointly owned by Authentic Brands Group and Footwork Productions, controlled by David Beckham.

Corey Salter, the chief executive of entertainment at Authentic Brands, said Beckham was “one of the most powerful global brands in sport, lifestyle, entertainment and much more”.

Salter added: “What these results show is that behind the Beckham brand is a strong and highly effective team within Authentic, set up with the financial discipline and strong fundamentals to continue to grow profitably through 2026 and beyond.”

DRJB Holdings includes the Seven Global division, which contains licensing agreements with companies such as Adidas. The remainder of the business is Studio 99, the production company that made the four-part Netflix documentary Beckham that was released in 2023. It also produced Victoria Beckham’s Netflix documentary, which was released last year.

David Beckham is also an investor in businesses including the supplement specialist IM8, which he co-founded in 2024, and the honey-based fruit snack firm BeeUp.

Sports.title: Manchester City guilty of breaching Premier League’s financial fair play rules – live reaction
Sports.text:
Business as usual on the Manchester City official socials, with this release timed for 5.30pm UK time: “Say hello to Little Beast, another addition to @MedlockSQ‘s restaurant collection! 🍽️ The menu evolves with the seasons, reflecting the changing produce, flavours and stories each full moon brings and is open every day 8:00-20:00 (UK) 🌙”

Looks delicious, to be fair.

Jake gets in touch: “Let us take today’s decision as a moment to reflect on the serious reforms that must be made in football. The staggering number of financial improprieties that Manchester City have been found guilty of has irreparably damaged the spirit of the game. The sacred trust we supporters have in the ideal of fair play is now worn threadbare and in dire need of repair. All we can hope for is that the Premier League has the ability to restore our faith that this beloved game is being played on as even a field as possible and that, going forward, athletic merit alone will be the deciding factor in determining success.”

An updated explainer on the Manchester City case, via Paul MacInnes and Jamie Jackson.

double quotation markWhat are the accusations?

In February 2023 the Premier League charged the club with more than 100 rule breaches, after investigating the club since 2019. The charges cover four areas: a failure to give “a true and fair view of the club’s financial position”; a failure to “include full details” of player and manager remuneration; breaches of national and continental financial fair play regulations; and a failure to “cooperate with, and assist, the Premier League in its investigations”. The counts have been heard by a three-person independent commission, with the process starting in September 2024.

While we rubberneck the City situation, some stories you might have missed.

A lucky escape?

Via the Associated Press: City did not confirm the decision, saying its case with the Premier League was “ongoing” and yet to be completed. City, however, would appeal a guilty decision and the process would take several months, a person with knowledge of the situation told AP. The person spoke on condition of anonymity to respect confidentiality elements of the process.”

As further background, a David Conn background piece from 2020, on the original Der Spiegel Football Leaks case.

double quotation markThe emails, splashed by Spiegel with evident relish across a series of exposés, punched into City’s expertly and expensively created modern image in three broad areas relating to Uefa’s financial fair play rules, which were introduced in 2011 to deter clubs from overspending.

First, and most damaging, were emails and accounting documents which appeared to show that City’s owner, Sheikh Mansour, of the Abu Dhabi ruling family, was mostly funding the huge, £67.5m annual sponsorship of the club’s shirt, stadium and academy by his country’s airline, Etihad. That created a perception that the Abu Dhabi hierarchy, in their drive to mega-spend on City attaining elite status while somehow complying with FFP rules, had deceived Uefa in their financial submissions. This serious trouble for City sprang from a tiny number of emails, a fraction of the documentary dump provided to Spiegel by its source, Rui Pinto.

double quotation markNB: Following the publication of the leaks, City refused to respond at all to Spiegel, the rest of the media and to Uefa, until the IC, having initially responded uncertainly, decided it had to investigate. City denounced the use of the emails as “out-of-context materials purportedly hacked or stolen”, and alleged there was an “organised and clear attempt to damage the club’s reputation”.

What sanctions may await? Some recent case law, via Reuters: “Everton were docked a total of eight points during the 2023-24 season after two separate breaches ​of the Premier League’s Profitability and ‌Sustainability Rules, while Nottingham ​Forest were deducted four points for ​a breach of the same rules in March 2024.

“Newcastle United narrowly avoided potential sanctions after selling players before a June 30, 2024, financial reporting deadline to comply with spending regulations. The allegations against City are far broader and cover more than a decade, making the case unprecedented in scale. Lawyers, club executives and supporters across the league have spent years awaiting a verdict.”

From a Premier League rights holder: “Sky Sports News understands that the process is moving to the appeal stage. The Premier League is not commenting as this is a private and confidential process. It will not be providing any guidance.”

That suggests a long way to go in this process. To the lawyers, the spoils?

Jack Crosby gets in touch: “I know it is fun to see who came runners-up in the competitions which City won, but it does really open a can of worms in reallocating winners unfortunately.

”Take the 2017-18 season. United finished second, just 4 points ahead of Spurs. Both United and Spurs played deep into the FA Cup, and will have rested players ahead of their semi-final match-up which will have impacted their league results. If they were in a title race, the league games would definitely have taken priority over the FA Cup, and so reallocating a winner in a season where the race for 2nd place was relatively insignificant to what else was on offer for the clubs involved is nonsensical. Liverpool were 6 behind United and their end of season league form was atrocious as they prioritised the Champions League run which saw them lose to Real Madrid in the final.

“Unfortunately, the entire Premier League has been brought into disrepute. City should be stripped of their titles and removed from the league, but the titles should not be reallocated. The league should mark “No Winner” or “No Champion” as a permanent reminder of their negligence in allowing City to do what they did, and of City’s guilt.

“Just as the Tour de France has done so with drugs cheats, they have owned up and said “our sport was not clean, and we are as responsible as anybody for that” - the honour roll will always remind people of that.”

Steven Grundy gets in touch: “Do you think that the Premier League can survive this? Surely this decision voids all the special moments, notably the “Agueroooo” moment. If I were, say, head of Sky Sports, I would be livid.”

Feels like Georgie Thompson’s voiceovers may need to be re-recorded on the Premier League Years.

double quotation markLeading the City team was David Pannick KC, one of the foremost barristers of his generation, renown for representing the rich and powerful. Previous clients include Queen Elizabeth II, Boris Johnson, the kingdom of Saudi Arabia and more than one billionaire sheikh.

Lawyers may not earn as much as the Erling Haaland’s £500,000 a week but Pannick charges a none too shoddy £5,000 an hour. In 2019, Pannick charged £407,250 for defending Sheikh Hamad bin Jassim bin Jaber al-Thani, a former Qatari prime minister, involving a two-day trial, which the crossbench peer did not attend.

Some quotes from 2023 as the charges were brought. The wait since has been lengthy.

Pep Guardiola: “It’s ⁠the same as what happened after Uefa (charges), ⁠these are just charges. With Uefa the club proved ​it was completely innocent. We are lucky we live in a marvellous country where everyone is innocent until proven guilty.

Guardiola: “Let’s go. Don’t ⁠wait two years. Why don’t we do it quicker? In 24 hours, sit down with lawyers present. Let’s have it as soon as possible for the benefit of everyone,” he said.

City Chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak: “I hope people focus and judge them [the players] ⁠for their football, what they’re achieving on the pitch and what they’re achieving in every competition they’re in.

David Howell also got in touch: “Fifth in 2019-20, fifth in 2020-21; all else being equal (ceteris paribus, as the lawyers would no doubt put it), that’s two Champions League cash injections denied to them by Abu Dhabi, and how different does that club look now in an environment where they get those?”

John Welsh gets in touch: “The list of alternative winners between 2008 and 2023 makes quite fun reading...

2010–11 FA Cup: Stoke City

2011–12 Premier League: Manchester United

2013–14 Premier League: Liverpool

2013–14 League Cup: Sunderland

2015–16 League Cup: Liverpool

2017–18 Premier League: Manchester United

2017–18 League Cup: Arsenal

2018–19 Premier League: Liverpool

2018–19 FA Cup: Watford

2018–19 League Cup: Chelsea

2019–20 League Cup: Aston Villa

2020–21 Premier League: Manchester United

2020–21 League Cup: Tottenham Hotspur

2021–22 Premier League: Liverpool

2022–23 Premier League: Arsenal

2022–23 FA Cup: Manchester United

2022–23 Champions League: Inter Milan

“Congrats to Alex Ferguson, Brendan Rogers, Jurgen Klopp, Mikel Arteta, Jose Mourinho and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer on your league titles. Well done to Dean Smith, Maurizio Sarri, Erik ten Hag, Arsene Wenger, Mauricio Pochettino, Gus Poyet, Tony Pulis and Javi Gracia on your cup wins, as well as to Simone Inzaghi for ending Italy’s long Champions League drought.”

Stepping away from Manchester City briefly, this story, via AFP: “Switzerland has lost a second player from its Nations League squad because of years-old cases of fake Covid-19 documents .

“Breel Embolo will not join the squad in Scotland as planned, the Swiss soccer federation said Friday, due to fresh reporting in national media about his past case of obtaining forged test certificates in 2021. This decision aims to allow the team to remain fully focused on the next matches,” the federation said about the Atlanta United forward.

“Switzerland captain Granit Xhaka agreed with team officials last weekend to withdraw from the squad because he is implicated in an investigation of a doctor issuing fake vaccination certificates during the Covid-19 pandemic. Xhaka, the Swiss record holder with 152 caps, admitted getting the forged document in 2022 and accepted he made mistakes.”

Further detail from our news story:

double quotation mark“The unprecedented catalogue of charges related to five distinct areas of alleged rule-breaking. More than 80 charges related to a club’s obligation to act in “the utmost good faith” when relaying information to the Premier League and to give complete disclosure of any information requested. These claims pointed towards the league’s belief that City had given an inaccurate picture of the club’s financial situation and withheld documents that might have cast greater light on it.

“The rest of the charges related to alleged breaches of profitability and sustainability rules (PSR) and the related Uefa financial fair play regulations. Finally, 20 charges related to the club’s obligation to provide “full details of … remuneration”, with breaches being claimed in the rules relating to the payment of players and managers.”

Via Reuters: “The Premier League declined to comment. ‘It’s a confidential process, we’re not commenting at all,’ a spokesperson said.”

Story: City found guilty of breaking Premier League’s financial fair play rules

Here’s our story on Manchester City being found guilty of almost all charges.

double quotation markManchester City face substantial sanctions from the Premier League after an independent panel found they had acted in bad faith and broken numerous rules over financial fair play.

The Premier League did not issue a statement but sources confirmed to the Guardian that City had been found guilty on almost all of more than 100 charges. City are surprised at the timing of the news because they say the process is ongoing. It is understood the club intend to appeal against a guilty verdict, confident of winning.

A verdict has been reached more than three and a half years after 134 charges, which cover the seasons 2009-10 to 2022-23, were brought by the Premier League and more than two years since arbitration hearings began. From season 2009-10 to 2022-23 inclusive City won seven Premier League titles, a Champions League, three FA Cups and six League Cups.

Updated at 16.40 BST

Further detail, this via Reuters.

double quotation markThe Premier League referred City to an independent commission in February 2023 ​over alleged breaches of finance rules spanning ‌the 2009-10 to 2022-23 ‌seasons. The club have consistently denied wrongdoing.

Among the most serious allegations was ‌that City failed in each season from 2009-10 to 2017-18 to provide accurate financial information giving a “true and fair view” of revenues, including sponsorship income, and operating costs.

City hired lawyer David Pannick to lead their defence, while the Premier League was represented by Adam Lewis KC, according to ‌British media reports.

The hearing began on September 16, 2024, and concluded nearly three months later on December 6. The case was ​heard by an independent commission composed of three judges appointed by the independent chair of the Premier League Judicial Panel.

Ah well, there’s always Oasis 2027 on 4, 6, 8, 11, 12, 15, 18, 19, 22, 25, 26 June. Will the Etihad be a Premier League ground? Will the case be closed by then? So much left hanging, including why we got to hear about this now, when details remain so sketchy.

How now to view these key moments in the City timeline? City fans may not, but the wider world will view with an asterisk. There are legal avenues to follow but who can speak for the court of public opinion?

Manchester City timeline: September 2008 to present day

Here’s a timeline of events, dating back to Sheikh Mansour’s 2008 takeover.

Updated at 16.20 BST

Remember this quote from Jürgen Klopp, Guardiola’s big rival, from 2024 when asked about the interminable legal process on City’s charges: “If you organise a bus parade – I’m in! How long it takes, I don’t care!”

Could be a big night out in Liverpool. City won the title by a point in 2018-19 and 2021-22.

If this story has a whistleblower, it is Rui Pinto, aka “John”, who obtained the leaked documents. Worth noting at this point that City, in the Uefa case said those documents came from “illegal hacking and out of context publication of City emails” as part of an “organised and clear attempt” to smear the club.

City have always denied wrongdoing, they say is supported by a “comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence”.

Further background from AFP: “The root of suspicion came from leaked documents published by German outlet Der Spiegel back in 2018. Emails purportedly sent between top City executives showed the club had inflated sponsorship revenue from Abu Dhabi state-controlled airline Etihad and telecoms firm Etisalat by disguising direct investment from Mansour’s Abu Dhabi United Group as income.

“Other documents claimed to show off-the-books payments to then manager Roberto Mancini via consultancy fees from a club in Abu Dhabi. If City are found guilty, sanctions are likely to include a severe points deduction and possibly even expulsion from the Premier League.

“Everton and Nottingham Forest were both hit by points deductions in the 2023/24 season for single breaches of profit and sustainability rules.”

These comments from Pep Guardiola, from 2019 and 2026, seem pertinent.

He departed City in the summer.

Worth mentioning at this point that City were banned from the Champions League in February 2020, and that Uefa ban was overturned in the Court of Arbitration for Sport later in 2020.

Updated at 15.40 BST

Will City be stripped of titles? The 134 breaches of competition rules took place between the seasons 2009-10 and 2022-23, during which they were English champions seven times, their 2023-24 title coming after that. We can only speculate at this point, with neither Premier League nor club releasing a statement to confirm.

Speculation will be wild over what the sanctions might be, and City’s peer clubs are likely to have their own thoughts. Thursday saw a Premier League meeting between stakeholders. Consider the compensation that Everton were ordered to pay Burnley this summer, for example.

Further background via the Press Association: “City were referred to the commission in February 2023, at a time when they were en route to the third of four consecutive Premier League titles.

“The investigation which ultimately resulted in more than 100 charges being laid started back in 2018. City had been charged with failing to report accurate financial information for nine seasons stretching from 2009-10 to 2017-18, as well as failing to provide full details of former manager Roberto Mancini’s pay between 2009-10 and 2012-13.

“They were also charged with failing to provide full details of remuneration in contracts with players between 2010-11 and 2015-16, and with failing to co-operate with the investigation over a period from 2018 to 2023.

“The club said at the time the charges were laid that they welcomed the opportunity for a commission “to impartially consider the comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence that exists in support of our position”. Four months after the charge was issued, the club won the Champions League for the first time in their history. The commission hearing began on September 16, 2024.”

That an appeal by City has not been launched or heard means this long process, beginning with revelations from Der Spiegel in 2018, is not at an end.

An explainer here from 2024.

Via The Athletic’s David Ornstein, Manchester City have said this: “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023. The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”

A similar statement has run on The Times. Much more to follow … much more.

Updated at 15.18 BST

Manchester City 'guilty' of Premier League charges

Good afternoon, and there’s highly significant breaking news, with reports widely emerging that Manchester City have been found guilty of all but one charge of more than 100 breaches of Premier League regulations, though no details of any sanctions have emerged. The expectation is the club will appeal. The club were charged in February 2023.

With that my watch has ended, I hand over to John Brewin who will take you through to the fixtures later on.

This is a good read:

Kane: World Cup hurt takes a long time to fully get over

Harry Kane was also asked how he gets over the pain of not winning the World Cup:

double quotation markIt’s not easy to get over but you don’t have a choice. I think it is something that isn’t spoken about a lot but when you are in that bubble and in that environment for seven weeks in the same routine, highest pressure, biggest games and then you go out and all of a sudden you are back to reality. Being a husband, being a father, you have been away from your family a lot so that takes an element of that away. It’s still there but you get back to normal life and enjoy being with your kids and they are the most importnant thing and they help you get over it. But it takes months, it takes a long time to fully get over it. You heal while you are moving on. There are still moments I think about it and I am sure the team think about what could have been, what if, especially meeting up again here and wearing the badge, it stays in your mind.

I think that is where tomorrow comes into it, the quicker you can put in good performances [the better] especially against bigger teams. So I think it is a good thing we are playing against Spain and Croatia and these top teams because if you do win those games I think it brings you back to the excitement of what is to come. Can we win the Nations League? Can we win the Euros in a couple of years? So I think tomorrow is important in terms of momentum.

Harry Kane added that Spain do play a particular way with possession and England players aren’t taught the same from a young age. But he says England have attributes Spain don’t and said:

double quotation markI think it is important to have our own indentity and not get caught up in other teams. That isn’t to say you can’t take things from other teams like probably club football you do as well. But ultimately it is about being England and showing our identity, especially in the bigger games as well.

Kane: This is my best chance so far of winning Ballon d'Or

The England captain Harry Kane said on if this is the best chance in his career to win the Ballon d’Or:

double quotation markBest chance right now yeah, whether that is in the future as well we will have to wait and see. I think so far in my career it is the best chance without a doubt. I spoke quite openly last season was my best from a personal point of view, it was my best year without a doubt. From a team point of view it was my best year in terms of trophies and performances. It’s something that would be amazing to win. I know there has been a lot of talk about it and I am sure there will be over the next month until it is announced. That is part of it. I would be extremely proud to win it. I did a lot of great things I can be proud of last year but ultimately it is down to other people now.

Michael has emailed his Taylor Swift entry:

double quotation markSheffield United’s trophy cabinet is just a Blank Space.

Tuchel: Palmer misses too many camps

Thomas Tuchel was also asked about Cole Palmer, who withdrew from England camp.

double quotation markMy understanding is he plays with discomfort and pain and he cannot compete on the highest level with discomfort and pain so he withdrew and informed us. Chelsea informed us, that is my understanding. We are not managing load.

When I was in club football I often used the term international break, this is when you hear it on the other side totally different picture. This is not an international break and I think that is what we created now. It is a competitive environment but it is also an environment that players love to be in. They love to train with each other and be with each other. That is what togetherness and brotherhood looks like. That is what we created from last September. We will never compromise on that. We will never let this creep in that players don’t want to come. It is fair enough but we focus on the guys who absolutely want to play for England.

For sure it is a missed opportunity and and it’s another opportunity, he misses too many opportunities. I don’t blame him for it, it is just a fact. He misses way too many camps with injuries. I only want to rely on what I personally witness and what I see within my team. If you are not in camp there is a next level to impress that you cannot achieve because you can only actually do it when you are with me on the pitch and with us on the pitch.

Five withdrawals came in the latest England squad for the team’s upcoming Nations League games. Thomas Tuchel was asked if he is looking into how to stop a potential culture of choosing club over country:

double quotation markFirst of all we trust our players and second of all I think the players know very well that if you miss a camp and if someone else is good in your position the competition will always be on. The door is always open and you have to make sure to be available and produce top level performances in camp and if you do so that counts for something.

Right now there is nothing to do. It is not on my list of worries. I am not wired like this. It is what it is. From the moment I arrive at SJP [St James’ Park] my full focus is on the staff and players. That is how I am wired. There is not threat, there is no distrust and there is no threat of consequence. It will come naturally.

I think we have the opposite, everyone is desperate to come. You talk to our captain who has the most minutes in club and country who is happy to be here while some teammates of him are enjoying a seven or two day break but he wants to be here. That is the role model that we have at the moment so there is no concern.

Tuchel says Alexander-Arnold will have 'chance to impress'

Thomas Tuchel was asked about Trent Alexander-Arnold and if he will start tomorrow against the world champions:

double quotation markOf course I will not tell you [if he will start against Spain]. He fights with Jarrell Quansah for the position and Jarrell played for us in the US.

Trent is up for the competition, we have very good training sessions and he was valuable and an important part of that. It’s not about words , it’s about actions. He will get his chance to impress and take back the shirt.

While we wait for Tuchel and Kane, have a read of the report from Australia’s almost famous victory over Brazil:

Josh has emailed and got involved with my niche Taylor Swift request. He says:

double quotation markGiven the relentless narkyness directed at Arteta-ball last season (and the pressure of 3 second placed finishes) I was impressed by the team’s attitude - just shake it off. They know financially compared to petro-teams they are dancing with their hands tied but for those of us in red that just makes it sweeter than fiction - karma almost. When you earn it like we did it hits different. Though I admit sometimes our manager behaves like the smallest man who ever lived.

I bow down to you, so many references packed into one email.

Updated at 13.53 BST

The England manager Thomas Tuchel and captain Harry Kane are due to speak this afternoon before the Lions take on Spain tomorrow. We will bring you any top lines from that when they drop.

This is an interesting read:

This may be quite niche but Taylor Swift has released new music today, in form of a Taylor song which best describes your relationship with your club? Spurs fans do you now have Bad Blood? Everton supporters was it a Cruel Summer? Let me know by emailing me.

Šeško defended after Rooney criticism

Slovenia manager Bostjan Cesar has come out in support of Benjamin Šeško after Wayne Rooney criticised the Manchester United player for his “little stupid shinpads”. The Slovenian is currently sidelined with a shin injury. Cesar said:

double quotation markIf you play for a club like Manchester United, these things come with the territory.

It’s a process that Beni isn’t going through alone. Everyone around him is going through it as well.

When he was fit and scoring goals, there were none of these criticisms.

He’s a professional and doesn’t need to pay attention to these things. He just has to try and stay positive and surround himself with the right people.

Updated at 13.19 BST

Some more news on Kai Havertz: As we know Havertz has returned to Arsenal but it is for a hamstring injury picked up during Germany’s 1-1 draw with the Netherlands in the Nations League on Thursday night. Early indications are that the issue isn’t serious. Arsenal will hope the forward is available after the international break.
